claims.text: CoCrFeMnNi is a high-entropy alloy suitable as the representative material for the proposed repair.
The damaged high-entropy-alloy component is susceptible to hot cracking during fusion-based repair.
Friction Stir Processing can repair the damaged interface while keeping the material below its melting point.
Tool rotational speeds of 500–1000 rpm are appropriate for the proposed repair.
Maintaining the process at approximately 0.5–0.6 of the alloy melting temperature provides suitable sub-melting repair conditions.
Friction Stir Processing induces dynamic recrystallization in the stir zone.
Friction Stir Processing refines the grains in the stir zone.
The process creates a dense and homogeneous metallurgical interface between the original material and the repaired region.
The resulting repaired interface is defect-free.
Severe plastic deformation during Friction Stir Processing causes dynamic recrystallization without melting.
Avoiding melting removes the liquid-phase pathway responsible for hot cracking.
Integrated in situ thermal monitoring ensures process stability and temperature uniformity across the repaired zone.
The FSP-repaired area will have improved fatigue strength relative to a traditional fusion-weld repair.
The FSP-repaired area will have greater resistance to crack initiation and propagation than a traditional fusion-weld repair.
The repaired microstructure will contain refined equiaxed grains.
Traditional fusion-welding repairs are prone to hot cracking in the proposed high-entropy-alloy component.
Traditional fusion-welding repairs produce inferior microstructures and mechanical properties under aggressive operating conditions.
The proposed repair can retain superior performance during cyclic thermal exposure up to 700 °C and representative service loading.
